topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-Preserving Architecture of Digital Contact Tracing
target_audience: University students (Computer Science, Data Privacy, or Cybersecurity)

sections.title: Introduction: The Privacy Paradox
sections.content: Introduce the challenge of tracking virus spread without creating a 'Big Brother' surveillance state. Define the goal of DP-3T (Decentralized Privacy-Preserving Proximity Tracing): notification without central identification.
sections.example: Characters Alice and Bob sit on a park bench. They want to know if they've been exposed to a virus later, but they don't want a central server to know they met or where they were.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Cryptographic Hash Functions & BLE
sections.content: Explain two building blocks: 1. Hash Functions (One-way 'digital blenders' that turn data into unique fingerprints). 2. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) (Short-range radio 'beacons' that act like a digital handshake).
sections.example: An animation of a 'Hash Machine' turning a secret word into a complex code that cannot be reversed. A visualization of Bob's phone emitting a faint blue pulse that only reaches Alice's phone 2 meters away.

sections.title: Local Identity Generation: The Rotating IDs
sections.content: Explain the hierarchy of keys: The Secret Day Key (SK) and the Rolling Proximity Identifiers (RPI). Use a graphical representation: SK_t -> [Hash] -> RPI_1, RPI_2... RPI_n. Emphasize that RPIs change every 15 minutes to prevent tracking.
sections.example: Alice's phone generates a 'Master Key' for the day. From this, it creates 'Temporary Business Cards' (RPIs). Just like a chameleon changing colors, Alice's digital ID looks different to every person she passes throughout the day.

sections.title: The Digital Handshake: Proximity Exchange
sections.content: When Alice and Bob are near, their phones exchange and store only the RPIs they heard. Crucially, this data stays *on the phone*, not on a server. Mathematically, the local log is a set: L = {RPI_received, timestamp, signal_strength}.
sections.example: Alice and Bob's phones 'whisper' their current 15-minute IDs to each other. Alice's phone saves Bob's random code 'X8j2' but has no idea it belongs to 'Bob'.

sections.title: Infection Reporting: The Decentralized Upload
sections.content: If Bob tests positive, he uploads his Secret Day Keys (SK) for the infectious period to a central 'Bulletin Board.' He does NOT upload his contact list. The server only sees a list of 'Sick Keys' but doesn't know who Bob met.
sections.example: Bob's doctor gives him a code. Bob's phone sends his 'Master Keys' to a public cloud. The cloud server acts like a public notice board in a town square where anyone can read, but the board doesn't know who is reading it.

sections.title: Local Risk Assessment: The Matching Process
sections.content: Every phone (including Alice's) periodically downloads the 'Sick Keys.' Alice's phone locally regenerates the RPIs from those keys and compares them with its own 'Heard IDs' log. If there's a match, the phone alerts the user.
sections.example: A visual split-screen: On the left, Alice's phone downloads Bob's 'Master Key'. It runs the 'Hash Machine' to see all IDs Bob used. On the right, it compares them to Alice's 'Heard IDs'. A 'Match Found!' pop-up appears only on Alice's screen.

sections.title: Summary & Key Takeaways
sections.content: Review the core strengths: 1. Decentralization (Matches happen on-device). 2. Ephemeral IDs (Prevention of tracking). 3. Privacy by Design (The server is 'blind').
sections.example: A summary graphic showing a shield protecting Alice's identity while a warning bell rings, symbolizing that she is safe and informed simultaneously.
